Toward the end of this process, you apply for admission into the nursing major itself. At that point, all they are looking at is your prior year (for an ADN/ASN) or two years (for a BSN) of coursework and related activities. As a result, pre-nursing programs tend to not be very competitive to enter. For some, admission to the college or university is sufficient. For ASN/ADM programs, anybody who can enroll at the community college can begin the pre-nursing program. I suppose it's possible that I'm wrong and that the college university you want to attend doesn't work this way. You need to find out where you plan to apply and what their expectations are. One thing that surprises me is that you're not taking an English class; you should make sure that you have enough English credits to get admitted. Generally, my point is this: you're thinking in terms of honors and AP being accolades that will be valuable, but that hasn't been my experience. many colleges and universities require that students take the three core natural sciences: biology, chemistry, and physics. If you have not taken physics but you have taken regular chemistry, you should probably take physics, regardless of whether it's AP, honors, or regular. I suspect that to maximize your chances of admission, your schedule should look something like this: pre-calculus, senior English, physics, history, and foreign language. Question: How do I tell my parents I’m struggling in school and want to switch schools?

Maybe write down a few points to help you remember how to describe your struggle. Is it grades? Social Issues? Not feeling like you're learning? Feel like you could do better elsewhere? Once you describe what the issues are to your parents, explain that you feel there's a need for change you can have your suggested outcome, presumably transferring to a different school (perhaps one identified), but your parents may have better advice. Now if you really feel that the solution is to a particular different school, you should outline why that school is a better choice for you in the short and long terms. Again, write this down before you talk to your parents; just winging it is not a great way for a child convince adults. Old_Answer: Money and connections. That's why these "volunteer abroad" programs only briefly had any impact on admission to the self-styled "elite" colleges and universities; they quickly realized that these were more functions of parents spending money than students really caring about digging Wells in South America or Africa. There are plenty of programs that will give you a volunteering abroad experience in exchange for a few thousand dollars. Whether the costs are legitimate or not, I don't know, but you will definitely travel to some other country and dig Wells or do something similar. Many churches have mission programs, some of which will involve students, but given the complexities of volunteering abroad and the tendency of young people to be… well, young people, you typically have to be involved for a long time. You don't necessarily have to be religious, I suppose, just involved in a mission group's work. What kind of costs would this require? Assuming you are connecting with an existing program, you can just act as a front. The costs are on the order of a few thousand dollars per student. If you genuinely want to build something new, I suspect it would require hundreds of thousands of dollars, plus connections. If your parents are involved in national government or international business, they can probably get you started. My suggestion is this. Pick something that you care about, and something related to your local community (construed broadly, so it could be your metro area). Then start volunteering. Once you start volunteering, recruit your friends to join you. Figure out how you as a group of young young people can have impact on your local community. raising a few thousand dollars great, but it's rarely a profound importance.
